text: A user with read access to an Incident can see its fields according to the Incident table's ACLs. It's easy to assume that access extends to anything attached to it — a screenshot, a log file, a document. It doesn't, automatically.

Attachments are stored and tracked through their own table, sys_attachment, separate from the record they're attached to. ACLs can be configured directly on that table — making read access to the Incident and download access to its attachment two separate permission checks, not one.

That separation closes a real gap. An Incident's attached file might be more sensitive than the ticket's own fields — a screenshot capturing a customer's full account details, say. The agent working the ticket may need full record access, but not download access to that one sensitive file.

Configuring a more restrictive ACL on sys_attachment makes that distinction enforceable. The agent keeps full, correct access to the record itself, while being correctly blocked from the one piece of it that carries extra risk — the attached file.

A nearly identical gap exists at the list level. A user with legitimate read access to thousands of records can open and read each one individually. Whether that same user can export that whole list to CSV or Excel is a separate question, governed by its own export capability and role requirement.

This isn't a formality. Viewing records one at a time in the UI leaves each view inside the platform's access controls and audit trail. A user who exports that data can walk away with it entirely — attach it to a personal email, copy it to a drive, take it anywhere outside the organization's control.

The data hasn't changed, but the blast radius of a mistake or a bad actor grows enormously once it leaves the platform's reach. That's why export deserves its own gate, separate from read access.
